_comment: Recorded Phase 03 Pre-Learning concept map for job 23 (the RNE golden chapter, 'The Rise of Nationalism in Europe'), authored exactly the way rne_prelearn.json and rne_place.json were: the pass was run against the real fixture chain with a recording provider, the premap payload it produced was dumped, and every concept below was written from THAT payload — the 16 merged prerequisites, their rationales, and the 15 source blocks they cite. The map is built from the capture and from nothing else: no post-learning concept row appears in the build payload, which is what separates this from the retired derive-from-existing flow (Q3). Each of the 16 captured prerequisites is mapped exactly once (R4); the grouping into 15 concepts and 6 topics is a meaning judgment, and only one concept consolidates two prerequisites (absolutism belongs in the same lesson as the forms of state it qualifies) — the rest stay apart because a lesson teaching them together would teach neither. Nothing is padded and nothing is invented to balance a topic. The needed-for links name post-learning concepts by TITLE, resolved against the request's own payload by the replay provider, exactly as rne_place.json names placement destinations; reading the Post Descriptions to LINK to them is a different act from building the map out of them. One pre-concept ('Finding Information Beyond the Textbook') carries an empty link list on purpose: no post-learning concept of this chapter genuinely requires independent research, and necessity is an ADVISORY critic dimension (Q10), so the concept ships with a review flag rather than being dropped. No Types, no Cases, no Examples, and no source QID appears anywhere in this fixture — the Pre lane never lifts a question out of the source (owner steer, 17 Aug 2026). Authored in TWO passes, and the second one is disclosed here because it is why this fixture draws three advisory flags rather than seventeen: the first pass wrote 134-239-word descriptions, well outside the 49-109 words the run's OWN Post descriptions occupy, so every row tripped concept_validator's `description_length` band. The second pass rewrote all 15 descriptions into that same band. That is authoring to the house standard the doc asks for ("the same detailing standard as Post-Learning" is a standard about the writing), not authoring to a threshold — but it does mean the advisory `description_length` path is NOT exercised by this fixture, and it is deliberately pinned separately, with a synthetic long paragraph, in tests/test_phase3_premap.py's validator-findings-flag-and-never-gate regression. The two flags this fixture DOES draw from the validator (`placeholder` on PRC-0001 and PRC-0013) were left standing on purpose: they are a keyword vocabulary in the SHARED validator firing on the ordinary English "none", a pre-existing Rule 1 defect, and the fixture records it rather than being massaged to hide it.

topics.title: Political Vocabulary of the Age of Revolutions

concepts.concept_title: Forms of Rule Before the Nation-State
concepts.description: A state used to be described by who ruled it and by what right. A monarchy is headed by a king or queen who holds power by inheritance; a dynasty is the family that passes that throne down the generations. A republic has no monarch: those who govern hold office because they were chosen. An empire is one authority ruling many peoples and territories joined by conquest or treaty. Cutting across all three is the question of restraint: absolutist rule faces none at all, so the ruler's word is law and dissent is repressed rather than answered.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Naming the form of rule a state has, and saying separately whether its ruler's power is restrained or absolute
concepts.keywords: monarchy, republic, empire, dynasty, absolutism, autocracy
concepts.rationale: One lesson teaches these together: absolutism is a statement about how much restraint a ruler faces, and it is only meaningful beside the forms of state it describes.

concepts.concept_title: The Plebiscite as a Direct Vote
concepts.description: A plebiscite is a direct vote in which all the people of a region are asked to accept or reject one specific proposal, usually that their region should join or leave a particular state. It differs from an election in what is chosen: an election picks people to govern, while a plebiscite settles a single question put to everyone. Its importance is consent. A territory taken by an army has been conquered; the same territory whose people have voted to join is said to have chosen.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Explaining what question a plebiscite settles, and why a ruler would want a territory's transfer confirmed by one
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.description: A vision is called utopian when it pictures a society so ideal that it is unlikely ever to exist. The word does not mean the vision is foolish; it marks the distance between the world as it is and the world the picture shows. Reading something as utopian changes the question you ask of it: you stop asking whether the scene records what happened, and start asking what its maker wished for, who stands together here who did not stand together in life, and what order the maker thinks the world ought to have.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Recognising a utopian picture of society and stating what its maker hoped for rather than what existed
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

topics.title: The French Revolution as Prior Knowledge

concepts.concept_title: The French Revolution of 1789 and the Transfer of Sovereignty
concepts.description: Sovereignty is the highest authority in a state — the power to make law that nobody within the state may overrule. Before 1789 it belonged in France to the king alone; the Revolution moved it to the body of French citizens, so law was held to come from the people rather than the throne. The sequence is worth holding precisely. Facing a financial crisis the king summoned the Estates General, the old assembly of the three orders; its Third Estate representatives, refused an equal voice, declared themselves a National Assembly of the nation.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Explaining where sovereignty lay before and after 1789, and telling the assembly the king summoned from the one that claimed to speak for the nation
concepts.keywords: French Revolution, 1789, sovereignty, Estates General, National Assembly, citizen
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.concept_title: Ordering Dated Events and Narrating a Sequence
concepts.description: Chronology is the arrangement of events in the order in which they happened. Working with it has two halves. The first is mechanical: place dated events from earliest to latest, read a span such as 1814-1815 as one event crossing a year boundary, and notice when two entries share a year. The second is what the ordering is for. A process is told as a sequence of stages, each taking up the situation the last one left, so a reader can follow how things changed step by step rather than meeting an unordered list of facts.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Placing dated events in order and retelling a process as a connected sequence of stages
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.concept_title: Telling a Cause from a Consequence
concepts.description: A cause is what brought a development about; a consequence is what followed from it. The two are easy to swap, so use a direction test: ask whether the item existed before the development and helped produce it, or came after it and resulted from it. Order is the other half. Causes commonly run in a chain, each link the consequence of the one before and the cause of the one after, and a chain retold in the wrong order becomes a different explanation.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Sorting the causes of a development from its consequences, and keeping a causal chain in the order in which it acted
concepts.keywords: cause, consequence, effect, causal chain, order
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

topics.title: Reading the Visual and Tabular Sources of History

concepts.description: A historical map shows how territory was divided at one moment in time, and it is read in a fixed order. Start with the key, which says what each colour, line and symbol stands for; nothing on the map means anything until it has been read. Then locate the states and regions the map names and follow the lines that separate them. Finally compare: with two maps of the same land at two dates, describe territory that changed hands, boundaries that moved, and names that appeared or vanished. A claim drawn from a map always carries its date.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Locating states and boundaries on a historical map using its key, and describing what changed between two dates
concepts.keywords: map, key, boundary, territory, comparison, region
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.description: A two-column table records a set of pairs. The headings name what each column holds, and every row states that the entry on the left goes with the entry on the right and with no other. Read it row by row rather than column by column: reading straight down one column gives two unconnected lists and loses the pairing, which is the only information the table carries. When you use such a table in an answer, turn each row back into a full sentence naming both halves and the relation between them.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Reading a two-column table row by row and restating each pairing as a sentence that keeps both entries together
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.concept_title: Reading a Figure's Number and Caption
concepts.description: Every picture printed in a history book carries a figure number and a caption, and the caption is evidence rather than decoration. It normally tells you what the picture shows, who made it and when. The figure number is how the running text points at the picture, so when the text says to look at a numbered figure, the caption is where you establish what you are looking at. Maker and date matter as much as subject: a scene drawn at the time by a participant and one drawn decades later are different kinds of evidence.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Using a figure's number and caption to state what a picture shows, who made it and when, before interpreting it
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.description: A caricature is a drawing that exaggerates in order to make a point. Its figures, objects and gestures stand for real people, institutions or ideas, so it is not a record of anything that happened. Interpret it in steps: list what is actually drawn; decide what each element stands for, using its labels, costume and any symbol familiar to the picture's first audience; notice what has been made too large or absurd, because the exaggeration is where the artist's opinion sits; then state the claim the whole picture makes.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Working out what the figures and exaggerations in a caricature stand for, and stating the opinion it argues
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.concept_title: Summarising a Passage in Your Own Words
concepts.description: To summarise a passage is to state its argument compactly in your own language. Find the claim the passage is making — the thing it wants the reader to accept — and separate it from the material that supports the claim, such as examples, figures and quoted detail. Your summary keeps the claim and the shape of its support and drops the illustration. Writing it in your own words is what makes it a summary rather than an extract, and the author's meaning and emphasis must survive unchanged.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Stating the argument of a passage compactly in your own words without altering the author's claim
concepts.keywords: summary, argument, own words, main point
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.concept_title: Separating a Report from the Reporter's Opinion
concepts.description: A written source usually does two things at once: it reports what the writer saw or knew, and it comments on it. Reported material can in principle be checked against other sources — what happened, where, when, to whom. Opinion is the writer's judgment of that material, and it shows in the words chosen to describe people and actions, in what is called just or shameful, and in what is left out. Neither part is worthless, but attributing the writer's judgment to the events themselves is a misreading.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Separating what a source reports from the reporter's own judgment, and naming whose view a quoted opinion is
concepts.keywords: source, report, opinion, viewpoint, evidence, attribution
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.concept_title: Reading a Quantified Statement Exactly as Worded
concepts.description: Historical writing is careful with quantity, and the words that carry it — all, most, many, some, a few, almost none — are part of the claim rather than decoration. Widening one turns the statement into a different and usually false one: 'most of the population were peasants' does not license 'everyone was a peasant'. The same care applies to scope: a claim made about one region, one decade or one social group holds for that region, decade or group and not automatically for a whole continent or century.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Restating a claim with its quantifier and its geographical, social and time boundaries unchanged
concepts.keywords: quantifier, scope, precision, most, some, all
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.description: An eyewitness account is continuous prose written as 'I', by someone present at what is described. Writing one means holding a single viewpoint throughout: the writer reports only what that person could plausibly have seen, heard or been told, in the order it reached them, and says how they felt about it. It is written in flowing paragraphs, not notes, and it never steps outside the person to explain what historians later concluded. Everything reported must fit what is known of the time and place.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Writing a sustained first-person account that holds one witness's viewpoint and fits what is known of the period
concepts.keywords: eyewitness, first person, account, continuous prose, viewpoint
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own

concepts.description: Some questions cannot be answered from the chapter in front of you, and answering them is a skill of its own. Turn the question into the specific thing you need to find out, decide what kind of source would hold it — a reference book, an atlas, a library catalogue, an archive, a person who would know — and go to that kind of source rather than reading generally and hoping. Record what you find together with where it came from, so it can be traced back and checked.
concepts.achieving_mastery: Choosing the right kind of source for a question the textbook does not answer, and recording what is found with where it came from
concepts.keywords: research, sources, library, reference, gathering information
concepts.rationale: a single captured prerequisite taught on its own
